identification.title: Christ Our Hope in Life and Death
identification.artist: Keith & Kristyn Getty and Matt Papa
identification.notes: Written by Keith Getty, Matt Boswell, Jordan Kauflin, Matt Merker and Matt Papa, copyright 2020 Getty Music, Messenger Hymns, Love Your Enemies Publishing, Matthew Merker Music and Jordan Kauflin Music; CCLI 7147502 per hymnary and PraiseCharts records seen in search results. The list's writer guess omitted Matt Merker. Built on the first question and answer of the Heidelberg Catechism (1563) on the believer's only comfort in life and death. Boswell and Papa had each been trying to write a song on that question; the ideas were joined at Getty's home in Northern Ireland and the song took over two years. Released by Getty Music in March 2020, and recorded by Matt Papa with Keith & Kristyn Getty and by the Worship Initiative with Shane & Shane. Reviewed as the song, not as any one recording.

claims.structuralNotes: Three verses, each followed by a refrain that is repeated at the end. The verses are built as a catechism-style question and answer modeled on the first question of the Heidelberg Catechism, and the refrain is a hallelujah and confession. The first verse says we belong body and soul to Christ, who holds our days and governs events, and whose love keeps us to the end. The second says God is good, his grace is known through the redeeming blood of Christ, and Christ is the rock who steadies faith in trials. The third meets death with the resurrection of Christ, promises everlasting life with him, and looks to his return, the rising of the dead, the destruction of sin and death and the feast of endless joy.

strengths.title: Honest about death, grounded in the resurrection
strengths.explanation: The song takes the catechism's question about dying seriously and answers it with Christ's resurrection, his return and the rising of the dead. Comfort rests on what Christ has done, not on the singer's courage.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Death swallowed up in victory through Christ - the answer the song gives to dying.

strengths.title: Grace known through the Redeemer's sacrifice
strengths.explanation: The second verse says God's grace is known through the redeeming blood of Christ, and that Christ steadies faith through trials. The cross is named and grace rests on it.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ - the source of the soul's calm.

strengths.title: Everyday life under God's governance
strengths.explanation: The first verse says we belong to Christ, who holds our days and governs events, and whose love keeps us to the end, which is the catechism's own theme.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Nothing separates believers from the love of God in Christ - the keeping the verse describes.

doctrinesAffirmed: Christ the believer's only comfort in life and death
Belonging to Christ body and soul
Christ's return and the rising of the dead
The final destruction of sin and death
theological.assessment: Nothing to correct was found. It answers the Heidelberg Catechism's first question in sung form: we belong to Christ, grace comes through his blood, and his resurrection, return and final victory give hope in death. The cross, resurrection and return are all named. The Spirit is not mentioned, which is an absence rather than an error.

strengths.title: Written as a shared confession
strengths.explanation: The song is a confession in the church's voice, answering catechism questions, and it was written for churches with choral and congregational arrangements published.

strengths.title: Fits funerals and times of grief
strengths.explanation: Its subject suits funerals, All Saints, Easter and any gathering facing death with hope.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Published keys were not checked. Test the chorus in rehearsal, as modern hymns of this kind often sit high for mixed congregations.

range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: One refrain returns after each verse and at the end, so the repetition anchors each stage (daily keeping, grace, resurrection) in the same confession.
communal.assessment: Congregational in design: short question-and-answer lines, three verses of moderate length and one repeated refrain, which makes it easy to follow. It suits funerals, Communion, All Saints and Easter.

strengths.title: Three verses with a clear arc
strengths.explanation: Daily trust, then grace in trials, then resurrection and the return, with a refrain tying each to Christ. A listener can follow where the song is going.

clarity.assessment: Clear. The question-and-answer form states each point plainly, Christ is named as the hope, and nothing invites a wrong reading.

synthesis.summary: A 2020 modern hymn by Getty, Boswell, Kauflin, Merker and Papa on the Heidelberg Catechism's first question. It moves from belonging to Christ and his governance of our days, through grace in his blood, to his resurrection, return and the end of sin and death. No concern was found.

scriptureReferences.relevance: Death swallowed up in victory - the third verse and chorus.
Christ's love keeping believers - the first verse's assurance.
Believers raised to meet the Lord - the third verse's hope.
Peace with God through Christ - the second verse.
No one snatches believers from Christ's hand - the first verse.
The feast and the end of death - the third verse.
